## Load Packages and Define Helper Functions

```{r load-packages}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(car)
library(glmnet)

summary_stats <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  x_c <- x[!is.na(x)]
  q1  <- unname(quantile(x_c, 0.25))
  q3  <- unname(quantile(x_c, 0.75))
  iqr <- q3 - q1

  vals <- c(N = length(x_c), Missing = sum(is.na(x)), Min = min(x_c),
            Q1 = q1, Mean = mean(x_c), Median = median(x_c), Q3 = q3,
            Max = max(x_c), SD = sd(x_c), IQR = iqr,
            Outliers = sum(x_c < q1 - 1.5 * iqr | x_c > q3 + 1.5 * iqr))

  data.frame(Statistic = names(vals),
             Value = formatC(vals, format = "f", digits = digits,
                             big.mark = ",", drop0trailing = TRUE),
             row.names = NULL)
}

# Side-by-side histogram and boxplot for one variable
hist_box <- function(data, var, label, fill = "lightblue", binwidth = NULL) {
  p1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30, binwidth = binwidth, color = "black", fill = fill) +
    labs(title = paste("Histogram of", label), x = label, y = "Frequency") +
    theme_minimal()

  p2 <- ggplot(data, aes(y = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = fill) +
    labs(title = paste("Boxplot of", label), y = label) +
    theme_minimal()

  p1 + p2
}
```

## Read the Data

```{r read-data}
# Read every column as text so listing IDs keep all their digits;
# numeric columns are converted below
listings <- read.csv("listings.csv", colClasses = "character",
                     na.strings = c("", "NA"), encoding = "UTF-8")

dim(listings)
```

> The raw data contain 4,368 listings and 90 variables.

## Select the Variables for the Analysis

The analysis uses the nightly price as the response. The main predictors from the proposal are accommodation capacity, bedrooms, bathrooms, room type and neighborhood. Additional variables that may also explain price are kept for variable selection: whether the bathroom is shared, distance to downtown, minimum nights, superhost status and the number of amenities. Some of these overlap with the main predictors, which will be checked for multicollinearity. The number of beds is not used: it is strongly correlated with accommodates (about 0.89), so it adds little information, and it is missing for 122 listings. Leaving it out keeps 91 more listings in the analysis.

```{r select-variables}
airbnb <- data.frame(
  listing_id     = listings$id,
  price          = as.numeric(gsub("[$,]", "", listings$price)),
  accommodates   = as.numeric(listings$accommodates),
  bedrooms       = as.numeric(listings$bedrooms),
  bathrooms_text = trimws(listings$bathrooms_text),
  room_type      = trimws(listings$room_type),
  neighborhood   = trimws(listings$neighbourhood_cleansed),
  latitude       = as.numeric(listings$latitude),
  longitude      = as.numeric(listings$longitude),
  minimum_nights = as.numeric(listings$minimum_nights),
  superhost      = ifelse(listings$host_is_superhost == "t", 1, 0),
  amenities      = listings$amenities
)

head(airbnb[, c("listing_id", "price", "accommodates", "bedrooms",
                "room_type", "neighborhood")])
```

> Price is stored as text with a dollar sign and commas (for example "$1,250.00"), so these characters are removed before converting it to a number. Superhost status is recorded as "t" or "f" and is converted to 1 (superhost) or 0.

## Bathroom Counts

The numeric bathroom column in the raw data is empty, so the number of bathrooms is taken from the text description, such as "1.5 shared baths".

```{r bathrooms}
table(airbnb$bathrooms_text, useNA = "ifany")

bath_text <- tolower(airbnb$bathrooms_text)

# Descriptions that start with a number, e.g. "2 baths", "1.5 shared baths"
has_number <- grepl("^[0-9.]+ ", bath_text)

airbnb$bathrooms <- NA
airbnb$bathrooms[has_number] <- as.numeric(sub(" .*", "", bath_text[has_number]))

# "Half-bath", "Shared half-bath" and "Private half-bath" count as 0.5
airbnb$bathrooms[!has_number & grepl("half-bath", bath_text)] <- 0.5

# Shared bathroom indicator: 1 if the description says "shared"
airbnb$shared_bath <- ifelse(grepl("shared", bath_text), 1, 0)
airbnb$shared_bath[is.na(bath_text)] <- NA

# Check the conversion: each description and the values it was given
bath_check <- unique(airbnb[, c("bathrooms_text", "bathrooms", "shared_bath")])
bath_check[order(bath_check$bathrooms), ]
```

> Every description that starts with a number is given that number, and the three half-bath descriptions are given 0.5. The 33 listings described as "0 baths" or "0 shared baths" are kept with a count of 0, as reported. The bathroom count includes both shared and private bathrooms, so a separate indicator, `shared_bath`, records whether the bathroom is shared (1) or not (0). The 29 listings with no bathroom description are left missing for both.

## Distance to Downtown

```{r distance}
# Straight-line distance (km) from each listing to Boston Common,
# using the haversine formula for distances on the earth's surface
downtown_lat <- 42.3550
downtown_lon <- -71.0656

to_rad <- pi / 180
dlat <- (airbnb$latitude - downtown_lat) * to_rad
dlon <- (airbnb$longitude - downtown_lon) * to_rad
a <- sin(dlat / 2)^2 +
  cos(airbnb$latitude * to_rad) * cos(downtown_lat * to_rad) * sin(dlon / 2)^2
airbnb$dist_downtown <- 6371 * 2 * asin(sqrt(a))

summary(airbnb$dist_downtown)
```

> Distance to downtown is measured in kilometers from each listing to Boston Common, using the listing's latitude and longitude. Distances range from 0.19 km to 14.4 km, with a median of 3.06 km. This variable gives a single continuous measure of location. It overlaps with neighborhood, since each neighborhood sits at a roughly fixed distance from downtown, and this overlap will be checked during variable selection.

## Minimum Nights

```{r minimum-nights}
summary(airbnb$minimum_nights)

# Long-stay indicator: 1 if the listing requires a stay of 28 nights or more
airbnb$long_stay <- ifelse(airbnb$minimum_nights >= 28, 1, 0)
table(airbnb$long_stay, useNA = "ifany")
```

> Most listings allow short stays (median 2 nights), but the minimum ranges up to 400 nights. Listings requiring 28 nights or more are effectively monthly rentals, and many hosts set the minimum at exactly 29 or 30 nights. These listings have much lower nightly prices: among listings with a price, the median price drops from \$236 or more for minimums under 28 nights to between \$119 and \$180 for minimums of 28 nights or more. The indicator `long_stay` is therefore added (1 = minimum of 28 nights or more). 1,817 listings in the raw data are long-stay listings, and 39 have no minimum nights recorded.

## Number of Amenities

```{r amenities}
# First few amenities of the first listing
substr(airbnb$amenities[1], 1, 70)

# Amenities are stored as a list such as ["Wifi", "Kitchen", "Heating"];
# count the items by splitting on the separator between them
airbnb$amenities_count <- ifelse(airbnb$amenities == "[]", 0,
                                 lengths(strsplit(airbnb$amenities, '", "',
                                                  fixed = TRUE)))
summary(airbnb$amenities_count)
```

> Each listing's amenities are stored as a list of text items, so the number of amenities is counted for each listing. Counts range from 0 to 93, with a median of 36.

## Missing Values

```{r missing}
colSums(is.na(airbnb))
```

> Price is missing for 882 listings (about 20%). Among the predictors, minimum nights (and so `long_stay`) is missing for 39 listings, and the bathroom count and `shared_bath` for 29. Accommodates, bedrooms, room type, neighborhood, distance to downtown, superhost status and the number of amenities have no missing values.

```{r remove-missing}
# Keep listings with a positive price and complete information on all predictors
airbnb <- airbnb[!is.na(airbnb$price) & airbnb$price > 0, ]
airbnb <- airbnb[complete.cases(airbnb[, c("accommodates", "bedrooms",
                                           "bathrooms", "shared_bath",
                                           "room_type", "neighborhood",
                                           "dist_downtown", "minimum_nights",
                                           "superhost", "amenities_count")]), ]

nrow(airbnb)
```

> Removing the 882 listings without a price leaves 3,486 listings, all with prices above zero. Removing the 64 of these with a missing predictor leaves **3,422 listings** with complete information.

## Room Type

```{r room-type}
table(airbnb$room_type)

# Combine private and shared rooms into one group
airbnb$room_type[airbnb$room_type %in% c("Private room", "Shared room")] <-
  "Private/shared room"

airbnb$room_type <- factor(airbnb$room_type,
                           levels = c("Entire home/apt", "Private/shared room",
                                      "Hotel room"))
table(airbnb$room_type)
```

> Only 4 shared rooms remain, which is too few to estimate as a separate group, so they are combined with private rooms. Both are rooms within a shared property, unlike entire homes. Room type therefore has three levels: entire home/apt (2,388 listings), private/shared room (977) and hotel room (57). Entire home/apt, the largest group, is set as the reference level.

## Neighborhood

```{r neighborhood}
airbnb$neighborhood <- factor(airbnb$neighborhood)

sort(table(airbnb$neighborhood), decreasing = TRUE)
```

> All 25 Boston neighborhoods remain. Dorchester has the most listings (482), followed by Downtown (276) and Back Bay (275). A few neighborhoods are small, especially Longwood Medical Area (17) and Leather District (3), so their estimated price differences will be less precise. They are kept so that every neighborhood is represented.

## Log Price

```{r log-price}
airbnb$log_price <- log(airbnb$price)
```

> Nightly prices are strongly right-skewed, so the natural log of price is added as the planned response variable for the regression models.

## Final Data Set

```{r final-data}
# Keep the analysis variables in a clear order
airbnb <- airbnb[, c("listing_id", "price", "log_price",
                     "accommodates", "bedrooms", "bathrooms",
                     "shared_bath", "room_type", "neighborhood",
                     "dist_downtown", "minimum_nights", "long_stay",
                     "superhost", "amenities_count")]
rownames(airbnb) <- NULL

dim(airbnb)
str(airbnb)
colSums(is.na(airbnb))
summary(airbnb[, c("price", "log_price", "accommodates", "bedrooms",
                   "bathrooms", "dist_downtown", "minimum_nights",
                   "amenities_count")])
```

> The final data set, `airbnb`, has 3,422 listings and 14 variables, with no missing values:
>
> - **Response:** price and log price.
> - **Property characteristics:** accommodates, bedrooms, bathrooms, shared bathroom (0/1) and room type (3 levels).
> - **Location:** neighborhood (25 levels) and distance to downtown.
> - **Listing and host:** minimum nights, long stay (0/1), superhost (0/1) and number of amenities.
>
> Nightly prices range from \$30.44 to \$4,815, with a median of \$250 and a mean of \$311, confirming the right skew. Unusually high prices are kept at this stage and will be examined during EDA and the regression diagnostics. Several predictors measure similar things (accommodates and bedrooms; neighborhood and distance to downtown), so multicollinearity will be checked before the final model is chosen.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

## Summary Statistics

```{r summary-table}
quant_vars <- c("price", "log_price", "accommodates", "bedrooms",
                "bathrooms", "dist_downtown", "minimum_nights",
                "amenities_count")

summary_table <- sapply(quant_vars, function(v) summary_stats(airbnb[[v]])$Value)
rownames(summary_table) <- summary_stats(airbnb$price)$Statistic

knitr::kable(t(summary_table[-2, ]), align = "r",
             caption = "Summary Statistics of the Quantitative Variables")
```

> Price has a mean of \$311 and a median of \$250, with a maximum of \$4,815 and 162 outliers, so it is strongly right-skewed. Log price is much more balanced: its mean (5.47) and median (5.52) are close, and only 32 values are flagged as outliers. The property characteristics are all concentrated at small values: the typical listing accommodates 2 guests with 1 bedroom and 1 bathroom, but each has a long tail of large properties, which accounts for the many outliers flagged for accommodates (304), bedrooms (217) and bathrooms (215). Minimum nights has a median of 2 but a mean of 14.4, because of a large group of monthly rentals. The number of amenities is the only roughly symmetric predictor (mean 37.17, median 37).

## Response Variable: Price

```{r price-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "price", "Nightly Price ($)")
```

> Nightly price is strongly right-skewed. Most listings cost under about \$400 per night (Q3 = \$393.98), but a long tail of expensive listings stretches up to \$4,815, with 78 listings above \$1,000. The boxplot flags 162 high outliers. Modeling price directly would likely produce skewed residuals and a variance that grows with price, so a log transformation is considered next.

## Log Price

```{r log-price-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "log_price", "log(Price)", fill = "lightgreen")
```

```{r qq-plots}
q1 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(sample = price)) +
  stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Price",
       x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Price ($)") +
  theme_minimal()

q2 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(sample = log_price)) +
  stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of log(Price)",
       x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()

q1 + q2
```

> The log transformation removes most of the skew. The histogram of log price is roughly bell-shaped and centered near 5.5 (about \$250 per night), with the mean (5.47) and median (5.52) close together. The number of boxplot outliers falls from 162 to 32, and they now appear at both ends rather than only at the top. The Q-Q plots show the same improvement: price curves sharply away from the normal reference line, while log price follows it closely except for small departures in the tails. Log price is therefore used as the response variable.

\newpage

## Quantitative Predictors

### Accommodates

```{r accommodates-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "accommodates", "Accommodates", binwidth = 1)
```

> Accommodates is right-skewed. Most listings host 2 to 4 guests (Q1 = 2, Q3 = 4), with the most common value being 2, but some accommodate up to 16. The boxplot flags listings for 8 or more guests as outliers (304 listings). These are genuine large properties rather than errors, so they are kept.

### Bedrooms

```{r bedrooms-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "bedrooms", "Bedrooms", binwidth = 1)
```

> Most listings have 1 bedroom, and listings with 0 bedrooms are studios. The distribution is right-skewed, and listings with 4 or more bedrooms (up to 15) are flagged as outliers.

### Bathrooms

```{r bathrooms-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "bathrooms", "Bathrooms", binwidth = 0.5)
```

> Most listings have 1 bathroom, with a second, smaller peak at 2. Values range from 0 to 7.5. Because the middle half of listings has between 1 and 1.5 bathrooms, listings with 2.5 or more bathrooms, as well as the few with 0, are flagged as outliers.

### Distance to Downtown

```{r distance-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "dist_downtown", "Distance (km)")
```

> Most listings are within 6 km of downtown (median 3.34 km, Q3 = 5.85 km), and the distribution is right-skewed. The 42 outliers are listings more than about 12.3 km away, all in Hyde Park and West Roxbury.

### Minimum Nights

```{r minimum-nights-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "minimum_nights", "Minimum Nights")
```

> Minimum nights has two distinct groups. Half of the listings (1,696) allow 1-night stays, and most others require only a few nights. A second large cluster sits at 29 and 30 nights (808 listings), with smaller groups at longer minimums such as 91 nights. This confirms that the data mix nightly rentals with monthly rentals, which is why the `long_stay` indicator is included.

### Number of Amenities

```{r amenities-plots}
hist_box(airbnb, "amenities_count", "Amenities")
```

> The number of amenities is roughly symmetric, centered near 37 (mean 37.17, median 37), with most listings offering between 27 and 47 amenities. Only 3 listings are flagged as outliers.

## Categorical Predictors

```{r categorical-counts}
table(airbnb$room_type)
table(airbnb$shared_bath)
table(airbnb$long_stay)
table(airbnb$superhost)
```

```{r categorical-boxplots, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%"}
b1 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = room_type, y = log_price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Room Type", x = NULL, y = "log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()

b2 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = factor(shared_bath, labels = c("Private", "Shared")),
                         y = log_price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Bathroom", x = NULL, y = "log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()

b3 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = factor(long_stay, labels = c("Under 28 nights",
                                                          "28+ nights")),
                         y = log_price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Minimum Stay", x = NULL, y = "log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()

b4 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = factor(superhost, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
                         y = log_price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Superhost", x = NULL, y = "log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()

(b1 + b2) / (b3 + b4)
```

> Each of the categorical predictors shows a clear difference in log price:
>
> - **Room type:** entire homes (median \$297) and hotel rooms (\$394) are priced well above private/shared rooms (\$114).
> - **Bathroom:** listings with a shared bathroom have a median price of \$92, against \$292 for those with a private bathroom.
> - **Minimum stay:** long-stay listings (28+ nights) have a median of \$134, less than half the \$308 for shorter stays.
> - **Superhost:** superhosts have a somewhat higher median (\$287) than other hosts (\$225).

```{r neighborhood-boxplot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 8, out.width = "100%"}
ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = reorder(neighborhood, log_price, FUN = median),
                   y = log_price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "log(Price) by Neighborhood",
       x = NULL, y = "log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

> Median prices differ substantially across neighborhoods. Longwood Medical Area, the North End, Downtown and Charlestown have the highest median log prices, while Dorchester, Beacon Hill, Roslindale and Hyde Park have the lowest. Beacon Hill's low position is unexpected for an expensive area. It is driven by a single host who operates 71 of its 188 listings, so it reflects that host's pricing more than the neighborhood. The spread within most neighborhoods is wide, so property characteristics will also matter.

## Relationships with log(Price)

```{r scatterplots, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8, out.width = "100%"}
scatter_vars <- c("accommodates", "bedrooms", "bathrooms",
                  "dist_downtown", "minimum_nights", "amenities_count")

long <- data.frame(log_price = rep(airbnb$log_price, length(scatter_vars)),
                   stack(airbnb[, scatter_vars]))
names(long) <- c("log_price", "Value", "Predictor")

ggplot(long, aes(x = Value, y = log_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "log(Price) vs Each Quantitative Predictor",
       x = NULL, y = "log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

> Log price increases with accommodates, bedrooms and bathrooms, and the curves flatten for the largest properties, which suggests the increase in price diminishes as properties get larger (research question 1). Log price decreases slightly with distance from downtown. It drops sharply as minimum nights rises from 1 to about 30 and then levels off, matching the two groups seen above. The relationship with the number of amenities is weakly positive.

```{r interaction-plot}
ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = accommodates, y = log_price, color = room_type)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3, width = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "log(Price) vs Accommodates by Room Type",
       x = "Accommodates (guests)", y = "log(Price)", color = "Room Type") +
  theme_minimal()
```

> The fitted lines have clearly different slopes: the line for private/shared rooms is much steeper than the line for entire homes. This suggests that the price premium per additional guest differs by room type, which supports including an accommodates-by-room-type interaction (research question 3).

```{r long-stay-interaction, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%"}
airbnb$stay_label <- factor(airbnb$long_stay, labels = c("Under 28 nights",
                                                         "28+ nights"))

i1 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = accommodates, y = log_price, color = stay_label)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3, width = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "log(Price) vs Accommodates by Minimum Stay",
       x = "Accommodates (guests)", y = "log(Price)", color = "Minimum Stay") +
  theme_minimal()

i2 <- ggplot(airbnb, aes(x = room_type, y = log_price, fill = stay_label)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "log(Price) by Room Type and Minimum Stay",
       x = NULL, y = "log(Price)", fill = "Minimum Stay") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

i1 + i2

airbnb$stay_label <- NULL
```

> Long-stay listings are priced lower overall, but the gap depends on the size of the listing and its room type, which supports keeping `long_stay` in the model through interactions:
>
> - **Accommodates:** the line for long-stay listings is about twice as steep as the line for nightly listings (a slope of 0.20 vs. 0.10 on the log scale). The long-stay discount is therefore largest for small listings and shrinks as the number of guests increases.
> - **Room type:** long-stay entire homes have a median price of \$184, against \$348 for nightly entire homes. For private/shared rooms the medians are \$68 and \$172, so the long-stay discount is proportionally larger for rooms. Hotel rooms have no long-stay listings.
>
> These patterns suggest including `long_stay × accommodates` and `long_stay × room_type` interactions in the regression models.

## Correlation Heat Map

```{r heatmap, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%"}
cor_vars <- c("log_price", "accommodates", "bedrooms", "bathrooms",
              "shared_bath", "dist_downtown", "minimum_nights", "long_stay",
              "superhost", "amenities_count")

cor_mat <- cor(airbnb[, cor_vars])
cor_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat))
names(cor_df) <- c("Var1", "Var2", "Correlation")

ggplot(cor_df, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Correlation, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "salmon",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation Heat Map", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

> The strongest correlations with log price are shared bathroom (-0.57), accommodates (0.52), long stay (-0.52) and minimum nights (-0.48). Among the predictors, the strongest correlations are between accommodates and bedrooms (0.81) and between minimum nights and long stay (0.78), followed by bedrooms and bathrooms (0.59). These pairs measure largely the same thing, which points to possible multicollinearity.

## Variance Inflation Factors

```{r vif}
full_model <- lm(log_price ~ accommodates + bedrooms + bathrooms +
                   shared_bath + room_type + neighborhood + dist_downtown +
                   minimum_nights + long_stay + superhost + amenities_count,
                 data = airbnb)

vif_vals <- vif(full_model)
vif_vals[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"] <- round(vif_vals[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"], 2)
knitr::kable(round(vif_vals, 2), caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (Full Model)")
```

> For a categorical predictor with several levels, `vif()` reports a generalized VIF (GVIF). The last column, $\text{GVIF}^{1/(2\,Df)}$, puts all predictors on the same scale as the square root of an ordinary VIF, so the usual cutoffs of 5 and 10 correspond to about 2.24 and 3.16.
>
> - **Distance to downtown** has the largest value (GVIF = 14.57, adjusted 3.82), above the cutoff of 10. This is because distance and neighborhood measure the same thing: once the neighborhood is known, distance adds little information. Only one of the two should be kept in the final model.
> - **Accommodates** (4.03, adjusted 2.01) and **bedrooms** (3.79, adjusted 1.95) are below 5, despite their correlation of 0.81, so their overlap is moderate and both can be kept.
> - All other predictors, including neighborhood (adjusted 1.07), are below 5 and are not a concern.
>
> These results will guide the variable selection step.

\newpage

# Modeling

## Reference Levels

```{r reference-levels}
# Neighborhood coefficients are measured relative to Downtown;
# room type coefficients relative to entire homes
airbnb$neighborhood <- relevel(airbnb$neighborhood, ref = "Downtown")

# Room type by long stay interaction. No hotel rooms are long-stay listings,
# so the interaction exists only for private/shared rooms: 1 for a long-stay
# private/shared room, 0 otherwise
airbnb$private_long_stay <- ifelse(airbnb$room_type == "Private/shared room" &
                                     airbnb$long_stay == 1, 1, 0)
table(airbnb$room_type, airbnb$long_stay)
levels(airbnb$room_type)[1]
levels(airbnb$neighborhood)[1]
```

> Each categorical predictor enters the model as a set of 0/1 indicators, with one category left out as the reference level. Every coefficient for that predictor is then a price difference compared with the reference category. Downtown is used as the reference neighborhood because it is central, well known and has many listings (276), so the neighborhood coefficients can be read as price differences from Downtown. Entire home/apt remains the reference room type.
>
> The EDA suggested that the long-stay discount differs by room type. None of the 57 hotel rooms are long-stay listings, so this interaction can only be estimated for private/shared rooms. It is therefore entered as a single indicator, `private_long_stay`, equal to 1 for the 406 long-stay private/shared rooms. This is equivalent to a room type by long stay interaction, without a hotel room term that would contain only zeros.

## Train/Test Split

```{r split}
set.seed(552)
n <- nrow(airbnb)
train_index <- sample(1:n, size = round(0.8 * n))

train <- airbnb[train_index, ]
test  <- airbnb[-train_index, ]

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

> The 3,422 listings are randomly split into a training set of 2,738 listings (80%) and a test set of 684 listings (20%), using a fixed seed. All model fitting, variable selection and cross-validation use only the training set. The test set is kept aside to measure the prediction error of the final model on listings it has never seen.

## Full Candidate Model

```{r full-model}
full_formula <- log_price ~ accommodates + I(accommodates^2) + bedrooms +
  bathrooms + shared_bath + room_type + neighborhood + dist_downtown +
  minimum_nights + long_stay + superhost + amenities_count +
  accommodates:room_type + accommodates:long_stay + private_long_stay

full <- lm(full_formula, data = train)
summary(full)$r.squared
summary(full)$adj.r.squared

summary(full)
```

> The full candidate model includes every predictor, a quadratic term in accommodates to allow the price increase to diminish for larger listings (research question 1), and three interactions: accommodates by room type (research question 3), accommodates by long stay, and the private room by long stay indicator. It explains about 74% of the variation in log price on the training data ($R^2 = 0.740$, adjusted $R^2 = 0.736$).

## Stepwise Selection

```{r stepwise}
n_train <- nrow(train)
null_model <- lm(log_price ~ 1, data = train)

# Backward elimination using AIC
back_aic <- step(full, direction = "backward", trace = 0)

# Backward elimination using BIC
back_bic <- step(full, direction = "backward", k = log(n_train), trace = 0)

# Forward selection using BIC, starting from the intercept-only model
fwd_bic <- step(null_model, scope = list(lower = ~1, upper = full_formula),
                direction = "forward", k = log(n_train), trace = 0)

# Term labels, written so that a:b and b:a count as the same interaction
term_list <- function(model) {
  labels <- attr(terms(model), "term.labels")
  sapply(strsplit(labels, ":"), function(z) paste(sort(z), collapse = ":"))
}

# Terms removed from the full model by each procedure
setdiff(term_list(full), term_list(back_aic))
setdiff(term_list(full), term_list(back_bic))
setdiff(term_list(full), term_list(fwd_bic))

# Do backward and forward BIC select the same model?
setequal(term_list(back_bic), term_list(fwd_bic))

formula(back_aic)
formula(back_bic)
```

```{r room-type-test}
# Partial F-test: does room type (with its interaction) add to the AIC model?
no_room <- update(back_aic, . ~ . - accommodates:room_type - room_type)
anova(no_room, back_aic)

# Room type and shared bathrooms overlap strongly
table(train$room_type, train$shared_bath)
```

> Three stepwise procedures were run on the training data.
>
> - **Backward AIC** removes no terms: dropping any term would raise AIC, so the AIC model is the full model, with 40 coefficients.
> - **Backward BIC** uses a much larger penalty per coefficient ($\log(2738) = 7.91$ instead of 2) and removes three terms: room type, accommodates by room type, and accommodates by long stay. This leaves 35 coefficients.
> - **Forward BIC**, starting from the intercept-only model, arrives at exactly the same model as backward BIC.
>
> Both procedures keep neighborhood and distance to downtown, the quadratic accommodates term, and the private room by long stay indicator. Because `private_long_stay` is a single variable rather than an interaction term, `step()` can keep it even after removing room type, as the BIC model does.

## Lasso

```{r lasso}
# Model matrix of all candidate terms (factors become 0/1 indicators);
# the column for hotel rooms x long stay is dropped because it is all zeros
x_train <- model.matrix(full_formula, data = train)[, -1]
x_train <- x_train[, colSums(x_train != 0) > 0]
y_train <- train$log_price

set.seed(552)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
plot(lasso_cv)

lasso_cv$lambda.min
lasso_cv$lambda.1se

lasso_coef <- coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.1se")
zero_terms <- rownames(lasso_coef)[as.vector(lasso_coef) == 0]
zero_terms
```

> The lasso adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients, which shrinks them toward zero and sets some exactly to zero. The tuning parameter $\lambda$ was chosen by 10-fold cross-validation on the training data, giving $\lambda_{\min} = 0.0005$ and $\lambda_{1se} = 0.0108$. Using $\lambda_{1se}$, the more heavily penalized choice whose error is within one standard error of the minimum, the lasso sets 11 coefficients to zero: nine neighborhood indicators (Bay Village, Brighton, Charlestown, Leather District, Mattapan, North End, Roslindale, South Boston and West End), accommodates by hotel room, and accommodates by long stay. A zero neighborhood coefficient means the lasso treats that neighborhood as priced like Downtown once distance to downtown is accounted for: several outer neighborhoods, such as Roslindale and Mattapan, drop out because distance already captures their lower prices. Unlike stepwise selection, the lasso treats each indicator separately, so it can drop some neighborhoods while keeping others.

## Cross-Validation Comparison

All candidate models are compared on the training data with the same 10 folds. For each fold, the model is fitted on the other nine folds and used to predict the held-out fold.

```{r cv-compare}
set.seed(552)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = n_train))

cv_error <- function(model_formula = NULL, lasso = FALSE) {
  pred_err <- numeric(n_train)
  for (k in 1:10) {
    test_idx <- which(folds == k)
    if (lasso) {
      fit <- cv.glmnet(x_train[-test_idx, ], y_train[-test_idx], alpha = 1,
                       nfolds = 10)
      pred <- predict(fit, newx = x_train[test_idx, ], s = "lambda.1se")
    } else {
      fit <- lm(model_formula, data = train[-test_idx, ])
      pred <- predict(fit, newdata = train[test_idx, ])
    }
    pred_err[test_idx] <- y_train[test_idx] - pred
  }
  c(PRESS = sum(pred_err^2), RMSE = sqrt(mean(pred_err^2)))
}

set.seed(552)
cv_results <- rbind(
  "Full model"   = cv_error(formula(full)),
  "Backward AIC" = cv_error(formula(back_aic)),
  "Backward BIC" = cv_error(formula(back_bic)),
  "Forward BIC"  = cv_error(formula(fwd_bic)),
  "Lasso (1se)"  = cv_error(lasso = TRUE))

n_terms <- c(length(coef(full)) - sum(is.na(coef(full))),
             length(coef(back_aic)) - sum(is.na(coef(back_aic))),
             length(coef(back_bic)) - sum(is.na(coef(back_bic))),
             length(coef(fwd_bic)) - sum(is.na(coef(fwd_bic))),
             sum(as.vector(lasso_coef) != 0)) - 1

knitr::kable(cbind(Coefficients = n_terms, round(cv_results, 4)),
             caption = "10-Fold Cross-Validation on the Training Data")
```

> The backward AIC model, which is the same as the full model, has the lowest cross-validated prediction error (RMSE = 0.3903 on the log scale), followed very closely by the BIC model (0.3906). The lasso has the highest error (0.3991), because the $\lambda_{1se}$ penalty shrinks the coefficients more than is optimal for prediction here. The difference between the AIC and BIC models is very small, under 0.1%.
>
> **The backward AIC model is chosen.** It has the lowest cross-validated error, and it keeps room type and the accommodates by room type interaction, which are needed to answer research questions 1 and 3. The BIC model drops room type, but the partial F-test shows that room type and its interaction add significantly to the model ($F = 3.88$ on 4 and 2697 df, $p = 0.004$). BIC removes it because room type overlaps heavily with shared bathrooms: in the training data, no entire homes or hotel rooms have shared bathrooms, while 528 of the 777 private/shared rooms do.
>
> The AIC model still contains both neighborhood and distance to downtown, which the VIFs flagged as overlapping. This does not harm prediction, but the coefficients of these two variables have inflated standard errors and should be interpreted with caution. The chosen model will next be checked with diagnostic plots and evaluated on the test set.

\newpage

## Model Diagnostics

The diagnostics are carried out on the chosen model, the backward AIC model fitted to the training data.

```{r final-model}
final_model <- back_aic
summary(final_model)$r.squared
summary(final_model)$adj.r.squared
```

### Diagnostic Plots

```{r diagnostic-plots, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8, out.width = "100%"}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(final_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

> - **Residuals vs Fitted:** the residuals are centered around zero and the red line is nearly flat, so the linearity assumption is reasonable. The spread is roughly the same across fitted values, with no fanning out.
> - **Normal Q-Q:** the points follow the reference line through the middle and lower part of the distribution, but curve upward in the upper tail. The residuals are therefore somewhat right-skewed, caused by a small number of listings priced far above what the model predicts.
> - **Scale-Location:** the red line is roughly flat, which supports the constant variance assumption. The log transformation of price has removed the increasing spread that raw prices would show.
> - **Residuals vs Leverage:** no listing comes close to a Cook's distance of 0.5. The highest-leverage points (about 0.33) are the three Leather District listings: they are the only listings in that neighborhood, so each has a large say in its coefficient.
>
> Overall, the assumptions are reasonably met. The main departure is the heavy upper tail of the residuals. With 2,738 listings, the t-tests and confidence intervals are fairly robust to this.

### Multicollinearity

```{r final-vif}
# With interactions in the model, VIFs are computed per predictor,
# combining each predictor with the interactions it appears in
final_vif <- vif(final_model, type = "predictor")
knitr::kable(round(final_vif[, 1:3], 2),
             caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (Chosen Model)")
```

> Because the model contains interactions and a quadratic term, the VIFs are computed per predictor (`type = "predictor"`), which groups each predictor with the terms built from it. The adjusted values in the last column are compared with 3.16, the equivalent of a VIF of 10.
>
> - **Distance to downtown** is the only predictor above this cutoff (adjusted 3.80, GVIF 14.46), because it overlaps with neighborhood.
> - **Accommodates** (GVIF 80.21 on 8 degrees of freedom), **room type** (22.23 on 6) and **long stay** (24.96 on 4) have large GVIFs because each is combined with its square or interactions. Their adjusted values are only 1.32, 1.29 and 1.50, so this is the expected structure of the model rather than a problem.
> - **Bedrooms** shows moderate overlap (adjusted 2.04), and all other predictors are low.
>
> The remaining multicollinearity is between distance and neighborhood. It does not affect predictions, but it makes the individual neighborhood and distance coefficients less precise. This matters for research question 2, where the neighborhood coefficients are interpreted.

### Outliers and Influential Listings

```{r influence}
n_fit <- nobs(final_model)
p_fit <- length(coef(final_model))

stud_resid <- rstudent(final_model)
leverage   <- hatvalues(final_model)
cooks_d    <- cooks.distance(final_model)

# Number of listings beyond the usual cutoffs
c("|studentized residual| > 2" = sum(abs(stud_resid) > 2),
  "|studentized residual| > 3" = sum(abs(stud_resid) > 3),
  "leverage > 2p/n"            = sum(leverage > 2 * p_fit / n_fit),
  "Cook's D > 4/n"             = sum(cooks_d > 4 / n_fit),
  "Cook's D > 0.5"             = sum(cooks_d > 0.5))

# The 10 most influential listings
top <- order(cooks_d, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]
knitr::kable(data.frame(Price     = train$price[top],
                        Predicted = round(exp(fitted(final_model)[top]), 0),
                        Room      = train$room_type[top],
                        Guests    = train$accommodates[top],
                        Area      = train$neighborhood[top],
                        Resid     = round(stud_resid[top], 2),
                        Leverage  = round(leverage[top], 3),
                        CooksD    = round(cooks_d[top], 4),
                        row.names = NULL),
             caption = "Most Influential Listings in the Training Data")
```

```{r cooks-plot}
plot(final_model, which = 4)
abline(h = 4 / n_fit, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

> - **Outliers:** 127 listings (4.6%) have studentized residuals beyond $\pm 2$, close to the 5% expected by chance. However, 26 exceed $\pm 3$, more than expected, which matches the heavy upper tail in the Q-Q plot.
> - **Influence:** 142 listings exceed the Cook's distance cutoff of $4/n = 0.0015$, but none comes close to 0.5. The largest is only 0.045, so no single listing dominates the fit.
> - **Most unusual listings:** the largest residual is a private room in Allston priced at \$4,815, which the model predicts at \$234. This is very likely a data entry error or a placeholder price. Other examples include a North End entire home priced at \$1,454 against a prediction of \$140, and a West Roxbury private room priced at \$735 against \$159. The three Leather District listings appear because of their high leverage.

### Sensitivity Analysis

```{r sensitivity}
# Refit the model without the listings with Cook's D > 4/n
reduced_model <- update(final_model, data = train[cooks_d <= 4 / n_fit, ])

key_terms <- c("accommodates", "I(accommodates^2)", "shared_bath",
               "room_typePrivate/shared room", "long_stay",
               "accommodates:room_typePrivate/shared room",
               "accommodates:long_stay")
knitr::kable(round(cbind("All listings"       = coef(final_model)[key_terms],
                         "Without influential" = coef(reduced_model)[key_terms]), 4),
             caption = "Key Coefficients With and Without Influential Listings")
```

> To check whether the influential listings drive the conclusions, the model was refitted without the 142 listings with Cook's distance above $4/n$ (5.2% of the training data). The coefficients for accommodates, its square, long stay and accommodates by long stay barely change. The coefficients for shared bathroom and private/shared room shift in opposite directions, from -0.435 to -0.359 and from -0.143 to -0.271, and the accommodates by private room interaction rises from 0.049 to 0.066. Because these variables overlap, their combined effect for a typical private room for 2 guests with a shared bathroom stays about the same (-0.481 vs. -0.496). The conclusions therefore do not depend on the influential listings, and all listings are kept. ($R^2$ rises to 0.81 in the refit, but that is expected when poorly fitting listings are removed and is not a reason to drop them.)

## Test Set Performance

```{r test-performance}
test_pred <- predict(final_model, newdata = test)
test_err  <- test$log_price - test_pred

test_rmse <- sqrt(mean(test_err^2))
test_r2   <- 1 - sum(test_err^2) / sum((test$log_price - mean(test$log_price))^2)

# Typical error in dollars: predicted price exp(prediction) vs actual price
median_pct_err <- median(abs(exp(test_pred) / test$price - 1)) * 100

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = c("Training RMSE", "10-fold CV RMSE (training)", "Test RMSE",
              "Test R-squared", "Median absolute % error (test)"),
  Value = round(c(sqrt(mean(resid(final_model)^2)),
                  cv_results["Backward AIC", "RMSE"],
                  test_rmse, test_r2, median_pct_err), 4)),
  caption = "Prediction Performance of the Chosen Model")
```

```{r test-plot}
ggplot(data.frame(actual = test$log_price, predicted = test_pred),
       aes(x = predicted, y = actual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Actual vs Predicted log(Price) on the Test Set",
       x = "Predicted log(Price)", y = "Actual log(Price)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

> The chosen model predicts the 684 held-out test listings about as well as it fits the training data. The test RMSE (0.388) is very close to the 10-fold CV estimate (0.390) and the training RMSE (0.383), so the model is not overfitting. It explains 72% of the variation in log price in the test set ($R^2 = 0.718$), similar to the 74% in the training data. In dollar terms, half of the predicted prices are within 23% of the actual price. The plot shows the test listings scattered evenly around the line of perfect prediction, with a few listings priced well above their predictions, as in the training data.

\newpage

# Research Questions

The research questions are answered with three nested models. The train/test split was used to select and validate a model for prediction. The research questions are about estimating effects rather than predicting, and Models 1 to 3 were specified in the proposal rather than chosen from the data, so they are fitted to all 3,422 listings. Using the full data gives more precise estimates and narrower confidence intervals, especially for the smaller neighborhoods. Distance to downtown is left out because the VIFs showed that it duplicates neighborhood, which would make the neighborhood coefficients unstable. Long stay (with its interaction with accommodates), the private room by long stay indicator, minimum nights, superhost status and the number of amenities are included in every model as control variables, so that the property and location effects are not confused with differences in rental type or listing quality.

```{r pct-helper}
# Coefficients as percentage changes in price, with 95% confidence intervals:
# a coefficient b on the log scale means price is multiplied by exp(b)
pct_table <- function(model, terms) {
  est <- coef(model)[terms]
  ci  <- confint(model)[terms, ]
  data.frame(Estimate  = round(est, 4),
             p_value   = round(summary(model)$coefficients[terms, 4], 4),
             Pct       = round(100 * (exp(est) - 1), 1),
             Pct_lower = round(100 * (exp(ci[, 1]) - 1), 1),
             Pct_upper = round(100 * (exp(ci[, 2]) - 1), 1))
}

controls <- "+ long_stay + accommodates:long_stay + private_long_stay + minimum_nights + superhost + amenities_count"
```

## Research Question 1: Property Characteristics (Model 1)

```{r model-1}
# Model 1 with a linear accommodates term, then with a quadratic term
model1_linear <- lm(as.formula(paste(
  "log_price ~ accommodates + bedrooms + bathrooms + shared_bath + room_type",
  controls)), data = airbnb)
model1 <- update(model1_linear, . ~ . + I(accommodates^2))

# Does the per-guest effect diminish? Linear vs quadratic accommodates
anova(model1_linear, model1)

# Quadratic terms for bedrooms and bathrooms as well
anova(model1, update(model1, . ~ . + I(bedrooms^2) + I(bathrooms^2)))

summary(model1)$r.squared
summary(model1)$adj.r.squared

m1_terms <- c("bedrooms", "bathrooms", "shared_bath",
              "room_typePrivate/shared room", "room_typeHotel room")
knitr::kable(pct_table(model1, m1_terms),
             caption = "Model 1: Percentage Change in Price")
```

```{r per-guest-model1}
# Percentage change in price from adding one guest, for a nightly listing:
# going from a to a + 1 guests changes log price by b1 + b2 * (2a + 1)
b <- coef(model1)
guests <- c(1, 2, 4, 6, 8)
per_guest <- b["accommodates"] + b["I(accommodates^2)"] * (2 * guests + 1)
knitr::kable(data.frame(From_guests = guests, To_guests = guests + 1,
                        Pct_change = round(100 * (exp(per_guest) - 1), 1)),
             caption = "Model 1: Price Change per Additional Guest")
```

> Model 1 explains about 66% of the variation in log price ($R^2 = 0.659$, adjusted $R^2 = 0.658$) using property characteristics and the control variables. Because the response is log price, each coefficient $b$ is converted to a percentage change in price, $100(e^{b} - 1)\%$, holding the other variables constant.
>
> - **Guests:** the quadratic accommodates term is highly significant ($F = 73.71$, $p < 0.001$), so **the price increase per additional guest diminishes for larger listings**. For a nightly listing, going from 1 to 2 guests raises the price by about 10.2%, from 2 to 3 by 8.9%, from 4 to 5 by 6.4%, and from 8 to 9 by only 1.6%.
> - **Bathrooms:** each additional bathroom is associated with a 24.8% higher price (95% CI: 21.0% to 28.7%).
> - **Bedrooms:** once the number of guests and bathrooms is held constant, an extra bedroom is associated with only a 2.3% higher price in Model 1, which is not significant at the 5% level (CI: 0.0% to 4.6%, $p = 0.054$). Capacity already captures most of the size of a listing.
> - **Shared bathroom:** listings with a shared bathroom are about 41.9% cheaper (CI: -45.3% to -38.3%).
> - **Room type:** compared with an entire home, a private/shared room is about 16.2% cheaper (CI: -20.9% to -11.1%), on top of the shared-bathroom discount, and a hotel room is about 22.4% more expensive (CI: 8.8% to 37.6%).
>
> Quadratic terms for bedrooms and bathrooms were also tested. They are statistically significant ($F = 15.35$, $p < 0.001$) but reduce the residual sum of squares by less than 1%, so the simpler linear terms are kept for these two variables to keep their effects easy to interpret.

## Research Question 2: Neighborhood Differences (Model 2)

```{r model-2}
model2 <- update(model1, . ~ . + neighborhood)

# Does location add to the property characteristics?
anova(model1, model2)

data.frame(Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2"),
           R2     = round(c(summary(model1)$r.squared,
                            summary(model2)$r.squared), 4),
           Adj_R2 = round(c(summary(model1)$adj.r.squared,
                            summary(model2)$adj.r.squared), 4))
```

```{r neighborhood-effects}
# Neighborhood differences from Downtown, in percent and in dollars.
# Dollar differences use a typical listing: an entire home for 3 guests with
# 1 bedroom and 1 private bathroom, a 2-night minimum, 37 amenities, no superhost
nb_terms <- grep("^neighborhood", names(coef(model2)), value = TRUE)
nb_table <- pct_table(model2, nb_terms)

typical <- data.frame(accommodates = 3, bedrooms = 1, bathrooms = 1,
                      shared_bath = 0, private_long_stay = 0,
                      room_type = factor("Entire home/apt",
                                         levels = levels(airbnb$room_type)),
                      long_stay = 0, minimum_nights = 2, superhost = 0,
                      amenities_count = 37,
                      neighborhood = factor("Downtown",
                                            levels = levels(airbnb$neighborhood)))
downtown_price <- exp(predict(model2, newdata = typical))
downtown_price

nb_table$Dollar_diff <- round(downtown_price * (exp(nb_table$Estimate) - 1), 0)
rownames(nb_table) <- sub("neighborhood", "", rownames(nb_table))
knitr::kable(nb_table[order(nb_table$Estimate), ],
             caption = "Model 2: Neighborhood Differences from Downtown")
```

> Adding neighborhood to Model 1 improves the fit substantially. The partial F-test is highly significant ($F = 37.74$ on 24 and 3384 df, $p < 0.001$), and adjusted $R^2$ rises from 0.658 to 0.728. **Location explains about 7 percentage points of additional variation in price** beyond property characteristics.
>
> The table compares each neighborhood with Downtown for otherwise identical listings. Dollar differences are calculated for a typical listing, which the model prices at \$391 per night in Downtown.
>
> - **Outer neighborhoods are much cheaper:** comparable listings cost about 34% to 46% less than in Downtown in Hyde Park (-46.2%, about \$180 less per night), Roslindale (-45.8%, \$179), Dorchester (-44.9%, \$176), Roxbury (-43.3%, \$169), East Boston, Mission Hill, West Roxbury, Mattapan, Jamaica Plain, Brighton and Allston.
> - **Central neighborhoods are close to Downtown:** Fenway (-9.1%) and Bay Village (-14.4%) are slightly cheaper, while Back Bay (-6.1%, $p = 0.059$) and the South End (-5.2%) are not significantly different from Downtown.
> - **Two neighborhoods are more expensive than Downtown:** Chinatown (+22.1%, about \$86 more) and South Boston Waterfront (+17.7%, about \$69 more).
> - **Small neighborhoods are imprecise:** Leather District, Longwood Medical Area and the West End are not significantly different from Downtown, but their confidence intervals are very wide (for Leather District, -46.7% to +29.7%) because they have few listings.
> - Beacon Hill is 16.9% cheaper than Downtown, which partly reflects the single large host who operates many of its listings.

### Interactive Neighborhood Map

The neighborhood results from Model 2 can also be explored on an interactive map: **[Boston Neighborhood Price Map](https://vincent-attakpah.github.io/Boston-airbnb-price-analysis/)**.

> Each listing is shown as a dot, colored by its neighborhood's estimated price difference from Downtown. Clicking a neighborhood on the map or in the ranked list shows its percentage and dollar difference from Downtown, the 95% confidence interval, the p-value and the number of listings. Neighborhoods that are not significantly different from Downtown can be greyed out, and the differences can be shown in percent or in dollars per night for a typical listing.

## Research Question 3: Interaction Effects (Model 3)

```{r model-3}
model3 <- update(model2, . ~ . + accommodates:room_type)

# Does the per-guest premium differ by room type?
anova(model2, model3)

summary(model3)$adj.r.squared

knitr::kable(pct_table(model3, c("accommodates:room_typePrivate/shared room",
                                 "accommodates:room_typeHotel room")),
             caption = "Model 3: Interaction Terms")
```

```{r per-guest-model3}
# Percentage change from adding one guest (2 to 3 guests), nightly listings
b3 <- coef(model3)
base_effect <- b3["accommodates"] + b3["I(accommodates^2)"] * (2 * 2 + 1)
room_effect <- c(unname(base_effect),
                 unname(base_effect + b3["accommodates:room_typePrivate/shared room"]))
names(room_effect) <- c("Entire home/apt", "Private/shared room")

# Typical (median) price of each room type
median_price <- tapply(airbnb$price, airbnb$room_type, median)[names(room_effect)]

knitr::kable(data.frame(Pct_per_guest   = round(100 * (exp(room_effect) - 1), 1),
                        Median_price    = round(median_price, 0),
                        Dollar_per_guest = round(median_price *
                                                   (exp(room_effect) - 1), 0)),
             caption = "Model 3: Premium for a Third Guest by Room Type")
```

> The accommodates by room type interaction is significant ($F = 6.64$ on 2 and 3382 df, $p = 0.001$). **The price premium per additional guest is larger for private/shared rooms than for entire homes.** The interaction coefficient (0.0494) means each extra guest raises the price of a private/shared room by about 5.1% more than it raises the price of an entire home (CI: 2.0% to 8.2%). For a nightly listing going from 2 to 3 guests, the price rises by about 9.8% for an entire home and 15.3% for a private/shared room. The hotel room interaction is not significant ($p = 0.19$), as there are only 57 hotel rooms.
>
> **Is the difference large enough to matter in practice?** Only modestly. In dollar terms the per-guest premium is actually larger for entire homes (about \$29 for a third guest, at the median entire-home price of \$297) than for private/shared rooms (about \$17, at the median of \$114), because entire homes start from a higher price. The interaction also raises adjusted $R^2$ only slightly, from 0.7279 to 0.7288. The difference is real and statistically clear, but small compared with the effects of room type, bathrooms and location.
>
> In Model 3, the main effect of private/shared room describes a listing with 0 guests because of the interaction, so it is not interpreted on its own.

## Final Model

```{r final-comparison}
# For a fair comparison, Model 3 is refitted to the training data only and
# evaluated with the same CV folds and test set as the AIC model
model3_train <- update(model3, data = train)
test_rmse_m3 <- sqrt(mean((test$log_price - predict(model3_train, newdata = test))^2))

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("Backward AIC (selected for prediction)", "Model 3"),
  Coefficients = c(length(coef(final_model)) - 1, length(coef(model3_train)) - 1),
  CV_RMSE   = round(c(cv_results["Backward AIC", "RMSE"],
                      unname(cv_error(formula(model3))["RMSE"])), 4),
  Test_RMSE = round(c(test_rmse, test_rmse_m3), 4)),
  caption = "Prediction Error of the AIC Model and Model 3")

final_vif3 <- vif(model3, type = "predictor")
knitr::kable(round(final_vif3[, 1:3], 2), caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (Model 3)")
```

```{r model3-diagnostics, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8, out.width = "100%"}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

> To compare prediction accuracy fairly, Model 3 was refitted to the training data only and evaluated in the same way as the AIC model. It predicts almost as well: its cross-validated RMSE is 0.3940 compared with 0.3903, and its test RMSE is 0.3906 compared with 0.3878, a difference of under 1%. Model 3 is the AIC model without distance to downtown, so it uses one fewer coefficient (39 instead of 40), and it has no remaining multicollinearity: every adjusted GVIF is at most 2.00, and the neighborhood value falls to 1.02. Its diagnostic plots, for the fit to all listings, are essentially the same as those of the AIC model, with reasonable linearity and constant variance and a heavier upper tail of residuals.
>
> **Model 3 is therefore recommended as the final model.** It answers all three research questions, its coefficients are stable and interpretable, and it gives up almost nothing in prediction accuracy. The AIC model serves as a benchmark showing that the simpler model is not missing important predictive information.
>
> In the final model fitted to all listings, holding the other variables constant, each additional bathroom is associated with a 17.5% higher price (CI: 14.2% to 20.8%) and each additional bedroom with a 9.6% higher price (CI: 7.2% to 12.0%), while a shared bathroom lowers the price by 35.1% (CI: -38.6% to -31.4%). Superhosts charge about 6.4% more, and each additional amenity adds about 0.3%. Bedrooms become clearly significant once neighborhood is included, because larger homes tend to be in the cheaper outer neighborhoods, which hid their effect in Model 1.
